chapters.file: ch20 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
chapters.relation: Nelson argues that critics forget Soderbergh directed Erin Brockovich because they file his career under the art/commerce binary, and he uses Nietzsche's attack on the 'faith in antithetical values' and Derrida's deconstruction to expose such binaries (art/entertainment, independent/mainstream, activity/passivity) as gendered, hierarchical, and unstable. He then shows the film's real signature is a 'self-centered narration' totally focalized through Julia Roberts's Erin, so that a tension between the movie's altruistic content and its Erin-fixated form never resolves. The chapter treats the binary as a rhetorically useful but collapsing tool rather than a real opposition.

chapters.file: ch21 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
chapters.relation: Morton reads Schizopolis as Soderbergh's philosophical autobiography of identity, quoting Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding on memory as the ground of personal continuity to interpret Fletcher Munson's 'transmigration' into the doppelganger Dr. Korchek. Because Fletcher carries his own memory and nature into Korchek, he cannot escape his failed marriage (Korchek is sleeping with Fletcher's wife), confirming Lockean continuity: he 'cannot escape his own nature.' Morton ties the film's decayed language games and Elmo Oxygen's gibberish to a view that language masks action, and reads Fletcher's fate-frozen ending as identity surrendered to outside forces.

chapters.file: ch22 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
ch23 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
chapters.relation: Sanders reads Soderbergh's HBO series K Street as a paranoid meditation on appearance and reality set in a Washington lobbying firm, where James Carville and Mary Matalin play fictionalized versions of themselves and the reclusive owner Richard Bergstrom manipulates everyone from afar while endlessly rewatching Mildred Pierce. Through three unresolved mysteries and a 'house of mirrors' structure, the show dramatizes the characters' skepticism about their capacity to know reality and Bergstrom's moral solipsism. Sanders argues Soderbergh's run-and-gun docudrama form itself enacts the epistemic uncertainty, leaving the text radically underdetermined about whether Bergstrom is a con man, a pawn, or a phantom-chasing paranoid.

chapters.file: ch24 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
chapters.relation: Sterritt 'schizoanalyzes' The Informant! by arguing that its lying protagonist Mark Whitacre, an ADM executive turned FBI informant, is a nut psychoanalysis cannot crack because he has no unconscious depth: his self is Deleuze and Guattari's rhizomatic, depthless flow of desire with 'nothing behind it' (echoing Warhol). He reads Mark's compulsive fabrication as deterritorialization against the corporation-as-psychopath, links the film to the Socratic unexamined life and to William James's open, flux-embracing empiricism (via Cassavetes), and interprets the climactic collision of Mark's voiceover and dialogue as the film itself intervening as the ultimate informant.

chapters.file: ch25 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
chapters.relation: Tait gives a Fredric Jameson-derived Marxist reading of Ocean's Eleven, treating Danny Ocean's heist crew as a utopian 'figure of collectivity' whose diverse, cross-class, pan-American membership recalls the WWII combat film and rallies against Terry Benedict as the polysemous 'monster' (Jameson's shark in Jaws) standing for globalized capital displacing nostalgic American Las Vegas. He argues the victimless heist allegorizes a competing value system in which love, solidarity, and friendship trump money, restaging class conflict from Asphalt Jungle, Rififi, and Big Deal on Madonna Street. The film's utopian happy ending imagines redistributing wealth and 'beating the house' within the very system of late capital it critiques.

chapters.file: ch26 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
chapters.relation: Biderman and Devlin use Traffic's four intertwined characters to test Kantian moral absolutism, applying the three formulations of the categorical imperative: Helena's decision to have witness Eduardo Ruiz murdered fails universalization, while Javier's whistleblowing on General Salazar (motivated only by duty, refusing reward) passes the autonomy formula. They argue Kant handles these cleanly but strains on DEA agent Montel's revenge (treating Carlos as a means) and outright fails on drug-czar Robert Wakefield's conflict between two absolute duties, to nation and to his addicted daughter. Following Sartre's critique that the categorical imperative is too abstract for concrete dilemmas, they show Soderbergh siding with existentialist choice as Robert invents his own law and quits to save his daughter.

chapters.file: ch27 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
ch28 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
chapters.relation: McFarland reads Soderbergh's Solaris as a meditation on recollection, recognition, and repetition, grounding it in Platonic recollection (the Phaedo, the cave, and the Symposium's love as desire) and Augustine's Confessions, where memory strains toward an elusive beloved-as-God, the 'cruel miracle' of present absence. When Solaris materializes Rheya, Chris Kelvin first jettisons the 'bad copy' but then, tempted by Snow, embraces Deleuze's endless degraded repetition of copies to erase his guilt over her suicide. Against this, Gibarian voices a Kierkegaardian call (Repetition, Either/Or) that there are 'only choices'; McFarland faults Chris, like Odysseus choosing Kalypso's island, for choosing the deathless eternal present over the human world of forward-moving choice.

chapters.file: ch29 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
chapters.relation: Moses reads Solaris through Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation, arguing the sentient planet is a 'dream factory' that reproduces Kelvin's dreamed Rheya as facsimiles with no original, literalizing hyperreality and the precession of simulacra. He treats Soderbergh's remake-of-a-remake status and the final scene, where Kelvin and Rheya speak directly into the camera as Solaris implodes, as pure cinema collapsing reality and representation, life and death, in Baudrillard's 'end of history' implosion. Moses extends the reading to unnatural reproduction (Baudrillard's clone/matrix, the aborted child), pervasive surveillance and monitors, and post-9/11 affects of terror, nostalgia, and melancholia, concluding the film offers no escape from postmodernity, only a way deeper in.

ch31 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md

holes.name: Fredric Jameson
holes.what: American Marxist literary and cultural critic known for 'Reification and Utopia in Mass Culture,' postmodernism as the cultural logic of late capitalism, and reading mass-culture texts for their allegorical and utopian impulses.
holes.why: Chapter 25's entire reading of Ocean's Eleven is built on Jameson's concepts (the utopian figure of collectivity, the polysemous Jaws-shark, allegory/utopia, late capital), and no taxonomy philosopher captures this specific cultural-Marxist apparatus.
